By Nolan Kido · About this writing

Follow the rules, count a complete hand, and learn how price, position, ranges and stack depth shape a decision.

A long-form guide to standard no-limit Texas hold’em. Read it in parts or use the native outline. All worked hands and numerical models are fictional teaching examples. Study away from play; no wager or account is needed.

Card key: A = ace, K = king, Q = queen, J = jack, 10 or T = ten; ♠ = spades, ♥ = hearts, ♦ = diamonds, ♣ = clubs. A♠ Q♠ means ace of spades and queen of spades.

No-limit Texas hold’em looks simple because the physical procedure is simple: each player receives two private cards, five community cards may appear on the table, and players bet on four streets. The intellectual problem underneath is much richer. You rarely know exactly what another player holds. You must make decisions with incomplete information, compare uncertain rewards with uncertain risks, and continually revise your view of what opponents might have. The uncertainty is part of the game: another player can bet with a strong hand, a weak hand, or a draw. A confident guess is still a guess.

This guide explains enough rules to follow a no-limit hold’em game confidently, then develops the ideas that turn those rules into decisions: position, starting-hand selection, ranges, pot odds, equity, value betting, bluffing, effective stacks, tournament incentives, opponent tendencies, variance, and structured study. Formal rules and house procedures are distinguished from strategy advice throughout. That distinction matters because tournament procedures, casino cash-game rules, and online-room software rules can differ even when the underlying game is the same. The Poker Tournament Directors Association rules are tournament procedures. A cash room or online operator has its own authority. This guide concerns standard 52-card, high-only no-limit hold’em, not Omaha, short deck, limit hold’em, or casino table games with similar names. All people, cards, stacks, and amounts in its worked examples are fictional. They do not describe my play or results.

Choose your route

You can learn this game without betting money. Use cards, chips with no cash value, or the website’s fictional exercises. This is a long reference guide, not a reading assignment to finish in one sitting.

Choose a useful way to learn
What you wantA useful starting point
Understand the whole gameRead the rules and complete hand below, then return for the decision chapters
Learn one idea at a timeFollow the four foundation lessons, beginning with your first decisions
Check whether you can explain itTry two situations in the beginner checkpoint and use the repair link that fits
Look up something specificOpen hand rankings, the glossary, or the math reference

Preparing to try a game? Use the first-session guide for format choices, full cost, live and online procedure, and a first-month practice plan.

Start with a modest goal: identify whose turn it is, what it costs to call, and which five cards make the winning hand. Those are concrete skills. Knowing a label such as “equity” is less useful if you cannot explain a new example in your own words.

No-limit hold’em is a game between players. You win a pot by making everyone else fold or by holding the best five-card hand at showdown. The house may charge fees. A pot you receive includes chips you contributed yourself, so it is different from your profit.

The central learning habit is to separate a decision from its result. A well-priced call can lose. An unjustified call can win. Neither outcome alone establishes skill or a profitable strategy. Research on evaluating poker agents illustrates why noisy outcomes need careful interpretation; it does not establish how quickly a beginner learns.

The rules and action order

The objective

Each player begins a hand trying to win the pot, the collection of bets made during that hand. If everyone except one player folds, the remaining player wins without having to show the best hand. If two or more players remain after the final betting round, they reach showdown, where the best valid five-card poker hand wins.

This means that poker is not merely a contest to “make a good hand.” Sometimes a mediocre hand wins because everybody else folds. Sometimes an excellent-looking hand loses because the board gives an opponent something better. And sometimes two players have exactly the same five-card hand and divide the pot.

Poker versus the house

In a normal cash poker game, your strategic opponents are the other players, not a dealer representing the casino. Cash-game rake may be taken from pots, or a room may charge a fixed collection or a time charge. Tournament entry prices normally include a fee. Check the current schedule for the exact game. The cash-game costs guide works through fictional schedules; an operator’s commission page describes that operator, not every room.

That fee matters strategically because poker among the players is not economically zero-sum after operating costs. If two equally skilled players simply trade pots back and forth while the house repeatedly takes rake, their aggregate result after fees is negative. It follows that a strategy merely good enough to break even against opponents before costs may still lose after costs.

No-limit and table stakes

In standard no-limit hold’em, there is no fixed upper betting increment. A player with 100 chips remaining can wager all 100. A player with 1,000 can potentially wager 1,000, although only the amount matched by an opponent is contested between those two players. The practical limit is therefore the stack in play.

Suppose Alice has $80 and Ben has $300. Alice moves all-in for $80 and Ben calls. Alice cannot be required to find another $220 merely because Ben has it. Their heads-up contest is limited to $80 from each player, plus any previous matched contributions. The unmatched excess would not belong in a pot that Alice can win. Buy-in limits and rules concerning adding or removing chips are house matters, so a beginner should check the cardroom’s rules rather than infer them from the phrase “no-limit.”

Forced bets

Hold’em normally uses a dealer button and two blinds. The button marks the nominal dealer position and moves around the table. The player immediately to the left generally posts the small blind, and the next player posts the big blind. These are forced bets, meaning the players contribute them before choosing whether they want to play their cards.

Some games also use an ante, another compulsory contribution designed to put additional chips in the pot. Tournament structures may use individual antes or a big-blind ante.

A voluntary call, bet, or raise is strategically different from a blind or ante. Paying a blind does not signal that the player likes their cards. They were required to pay.

Positions

Position is usually described relative to the button.

Seat names
PositionMeaningStrategic character
Under the gun, or UTGFirst player to act preflop in a normal multiway handEarly position, many players remain behind
Middle positionsSeats between early and late positionIntermediate information and risk
HijackUsually two seats right of the button in common table namingLate or later-middle position depending table size
CutoffSeat immediately right of the buttonVery strong position
ButtonDealer-button seatActs last on normal postflop streets
Small blindLeft of buttonForced small bet, usually acts early after flop
Big blindLeft of small blindForced big bet, usually acts early after flop

The precise labels for “middle position” change with table size. At a nine-handed full-ring table there are several genuinely early seats. At six-handed tables there are fewer players between the blinds and button, so labels compress and strategically playable ranges tend to be wider.

Position is not valuable because the button somehow receives better cards. It is valuable because information arrives sequentially. Seeing an opponent check before you decide is useful. Seeing three people fold before you act preflop is useful. Being forced to decide first gives your opponent that informational benefit instead.

Action order

In a normal multiway hand, preflop action starts with the player immediately left of the big blind. If nobody raises, the big blind usually receives the last opportunity to check or raise before the flop. After the flop, action begins with the first active player to the left of the button, which means the blinds, when still in the hand, normally act before late-position players.

Heads-up poker is the important exception. The button posts the small blind, the other player posts the big blind, and the button acts first preflop but last on later streets.

How a hand unfolds

  1. Post blinds and any antes; deal two private cards to each player.
  2. Preflop: act before community cards.
  3. Flop: deal three shared cards, then bet.
  4. Turn: deal one shared card, then bet.
  5. River: deal one shared card, then bet.
  6. Showdown: compare the best five cards if at least two players remain.

Stop earlier if every opponent folds. If all remaining players are all-in, deal the remaining board without further betting.

Each player first receives two private hole cards. The first betting round is called preflop. If at least two players remain, three community cards are dealt together as the flop. A betting round follows. One additional community card is the turn, followed by another round of betting. The fifth and final community card is the river, followed by the last betting round. If multiple players remain, there is a showdown.

A betting round normally ends when every player still entitled to act has either folded or has responded to the current wager so that all non-all-in players have matched the amount required, with no further raise pending. An all-in player can remain eligible for a pot despite having no chips left with which to act.

A complete hand, with the pot counted

Consider a six-handed $1/$2 cash game. Ignore rake so the arithmetic remains transparent. Everyone relevant begins with at least $200.

The small blind posts $1 and the big blind $2. The first player folds. The next player, whom we will call Maya, raises to $6. The cutoff folds. You are on the button with A♠ Q♠ and call $6. The small blind folds. The big blind calls another $4.

The pot is now:

  • $6 from Maya
  • $6 from you
  • $6 from the big blind
  • $1 abandoned by the small blind

Total: $19.

The flop is Q♦ 7♠ 4♠. The big blind checks. Maya bets $10. You have top pair with an ace kicker plus a flush draw. For this bookkeeping example, you call $10. We have not supplied Maya’s range or response frequencies, so the example does not establish whether calling is better than raising or folding. The big blind folds.

The pot was $19. Maya added $10 and you added $10, so the turn pot is $39.

The turn is 2♣. Maya checks. In the illustrated sequence, you bet $24. A value-betting explanation would need to identify worse hands likely to call that size. Maya’s eventual revealed hand does not prove what you knew then. Maya calls. The pot becomes:

$39 + $24 + $24 = $87.

The river is 9♥. Maya checks. You bet $40. Maya calls and shows K♣ Q♣. Your best hand is a pair of queens with ace kicker; Maya has a pair of queens with king kicker. You win.

Final pot:

$87 + $40 + $40 = $167.

The contribution audit confirms the same result: Maya put in $6 + $10 + $24 + $40 = $80. You put in $80. The big blind contributed $6. The small blind contributed $1. Total: $80 + $80 + $6 + $1 = $167.

Your $167 pot receipt includes your own $80 contribution. Your net change from the start of this hand is $167 - $80 = +$87, before fees. At a later decision point, chips already contributed are sunk: compare the extra cost and payoff of the options still available. The hand illustrates action order, five-card comparison, and accounting. It supplies no optimal bet size or solver result.

Which five cards win?

Hold’em uses conventional high-poker rankings. The strongest valid five-card category wins.

Standard high-poker hand rankings
RankExampleMeaning
Straight flush9♣ 8♣ 7♣ 6♣ 5♣Five consecutive cards of one suit
Four of a kindK♠ K♥ K♦ K♣ 3♠Four cards of one rank
Full houseQ♠ Q♥ Q♦ 7♣ 7♦Three of one rank plus a pair
FlushA♣ J♣ 8♣ 5♣ 2♣Five cards of one suit
Straight9♠ 8♦ 7♣ 6♥ 5♠Five consecutive ranks
Three of a kind7♠ 7♥ 7♦ A♣ K♣Three cards of one rank
Two pairJ♠ J♦ 4♣ 4♥ A♠Two separate pairs
One pair9♠ 9♥ A♦ K♣ 7♠One pair
High cardA♠ K♦ J♣ 8♥ 5♣None of the above

A royal flush is an ace-high straight flush, not a separate category above straight flush. An ace may be low in A-2-3-4-5, but it cannot wrap around, so Q-K-A-2-3 is not a straight.

Your hand is always the best five cards that can be formed from the seven available cards: your two hole cards plus the five board cards. You may use both hole cards, one, or none. This point differentiates hold’em from games such as Omaha, where a fixed number of hole cards must be used.

Worked example: the kicker matters

You hold A♣ K♦. Your opponent holds A♥ Q♥. The board is A♠ 8♣ 8♦ 4♠ 2♣.

Both players have two pair, aces and eights. Your five cards are A-A-8-8-K. The opponent’s are A-A-8-8-Q. Your king is the kicker, the deciding side card, so you win.

Worked example: the impressive pocket pair is not the winning hand

You hold 9♠ 9♥. An opponent holds A♣ K♣. The board is A♦ 9♦ K♥ K♠ 2♣.

At first glance, your flopped set of nines feels enormous. By the river, however, your best five cards are 9-9-9-K-K, nines full of kings. Your opponent uses K♣ with the two kings on the board plus the two aces available from A♣ and A♦, making K-K-K-A-A, kings full of aces. Kings full beats nines full.

The label you gave your hand on the flop does not remain permanently attached to it. Every new community card can redefine both players’ best five.

Worked example: playing the board

The community cards are A♠ K♦ Q♣ J♥ 10♠. Everyone who remains has at least the Broadway straight A-K-Q-J-10 from the board itself. No hole cards can create a higher five-card hand. Assuming no special circumstance outside standard hold’em, the pot is split among tied players.

A similar principle applies to a five-card flush on the board. Suppose the board is A♥ J♥ 8♥ 5♥ 2♥, while one player holds K♣ K♦ and the other Q♣ Q♦. Neither hole card is a heart, so both players’ best hand is the same ace-high heart flush from the board. Standard hold’em does not award the pot to one player because spades or another suit supposedly “rank higher.” Suits are not tie-breakers for ordinary hand comparison.

Paired boards

A board such as K♠ K♦ 7♣ 3♥ 2♣ should immediately make you ask which five cards actually play. A player holding A♥ K♣ has three kings, while a player holding 7♦ 7♥ has a full house, sevens full of kings. The full house wins. These exact suits are legal alongside the board. A paired board also changes drawing risks: a flush that arrives on a paired board can still lose to a full house. This is one reason raw “outs” must sometimes be discounted later.

Legal actions, raises and side pots

Checking, betting, calling, raising, folding

A check passes the action without adding chips and is permitted only when there is no outstanding wager to call. A bet puts chips in when nobody has yet bet on that street. A call matches the current wager. A raise increases it. A fold relinquishes the hand and any claim to the pot. Going all-in means wagering all chips remaining in your stack.

Clear language prevents misunderstandings. Verbal declarations and gestures can be binding. Make your intended action clear; ask a neutral question such as “What is the amount?” before announcing an action. The TDA procedures explain tournament rulings; a cash room applies its own rules. Live cash rooms may have their own exact procedures, but “raise to fifty” is much safer than an ambiguous gesture with chips.

Raise “to” versus raise “by.”

Imagine somebody bets $10. You say, “Raise to $25.” Your total wager is $25, so you have increased the bet by $15. Saying “raise by $25” would ordinarily describe an increase of $25, implying a total of $35. Because spoken wording can be interpreted according to house rules, the clearest live declaration is generally the intended total: “raise to twenty-five.”

State the intended total clearly. In the 2026 TDA rules, an amount stated with a raise is treated as the total unless otherwise clarified.

Minimum raises and full raises

In no-limit hold’em, a raise normally must increase the wager by at least the size of the previous full bet or raise on that betting round. Check the room’s published rules and ask the dealer when a short all-in makes the available actions unclear.

Suppose Player A bets $10. Player B raises to $25. B’s raise increment is $15. If Player C wants to make a normal full raise, C must therefore raise by at least another $15, to $40 total.

An all-in creates a special case. Suppose C has only $32 and moves all-in. C has increased $25 to $32, only $7, which is less than the required $15 full raise. The wager is still valid because C is all-in, but that short increase does not necessarily reopen raising for players who already acted.

Under the 2026 TDA tournament rules, one short all-in, or multiple short all-ins whose cumulative increase remains below a full raise, does not reopen betting to a player who already acted and is not now facing at least a full raise. This is checked player by player. If A had bet $10 and faces $32 after B’s full raise to $25, A faces at least a full $15 increase and can raise. If A just calls $32, B faces only $7 beyond B’s last $25 action and cannot reraise solely because of C’s short all-in. A player who has not yet acted retains the option to raise. Cumulative short all-ins can reopen action for a player who then faces at least a full increment; the minimum increment stays the last full bet or raise. Many no-limit cash games follow a comparable principle, but this is exactly the kind of procedural point that should be confirmed with the house rather than treated as universal.

Side pots. Worked example

Alice has $40, Ben $100, and Cara $100. All three eventually move all-in.

The first $40 from each player makes the main pot:

3 × $40 = $120.

Alice, Ben, and Cara are all eligible for that $120.

Ben and Cara each have another $60 matched against each other:

2 × $60 = $120.

That forms a side pot. Only Ben and Cara can win it because Alice did not contribute to it.

If Alice has the strongest hand overall, she receives the $120 main pot, while the better hand between Ben and Cara takes the $120 side pot. If Cara has the best hand overall, Cara can win both pots for $240.

This is the precise meaning of “you can only win from an opponent what you can match.” Being short-stacked does not prevent winning a main pot, but it prevents claiming money wagered exclusively between deeper players. If Cara instead has $150 and pushes it all in while Ben has only $100, Cara’s unmatched $50 is returned. It is not a third pot that somebody can win. Folded players’ matched contributions stay in the appropriate pots. See the side-pot lab for more cases.

Starting hands and ranges

A useful beginner study question is which weak starting hands create expensive later decisions. Folding is a normal legal choice, not a failure to participate. That may sound unglamorous, but every hand you voluntarily enter creates the possibility of facing several more decisions with money at risk. Weak starting cards frequently make second-best pairs, inferior kickers, and draws that cost money to pursue.

Categories of starting hands

A pocket pair means two hole cards of the same rank, such as 8♣ 8♦. High pairs begin strong as made hands; smaller pairs can sometimes improve to three of a kind but can be difficult to navigate when overcards appear.

Suited cards share a suit. Suitedness improves the possibility of making a flush, but it does not transform any two cards into a good starting hand. K♠ Q♠ has high-card strength, connectivity, and suitedness. 8♥ 3♥ is suited but poorly connected and makes weak pairs. “They were suited” is therefore not a sufficient reason to play.

Connected cards are adjacent or nearly adjacent in rank, such as 9-8 or J-10. Suited connectors can make straights and flushes and can play well under suitable stack and position conditions. That does not mean they should automatically be called against a large raise.

Broadway cards generally refers to the high ranks ten through ace. Combinations such as A-K, A-Q, K-Q, and Q-J can make strong top pairs and high straights, though offsuit and dominated versions require caution.

Weak aces illustrate domination. Suppose you hold A-J and an opponent holds A-Q. On A-7-2, both players have top pair, but the opponent’s queen kicker is ahead of your jack. You can improve, so you are not drawing dead, but many apparently favorable ace-high flops leave your hand second best. This recurring problem is why A-5 offsuit and similar holdings are very different from A-K despite sharing an ace.

Established beginner strategy material likewise emphasizes that starting-hand value depends not just on the two cards but on position, stack size, previous action, and opponent behavior. Exact percentages or charts published by training sites should be treated as examples of strategies, not universal laws.

Position changes what is playable

Imagine eight opponents remain to act after you. Even if no particular opponent is very likely to have a premium hand, there are many opportunities collectively for somebody to wake up with one. You also risk playing the rest of the hand out of position. The same marginal holding on the button after everyone folds encounters only the two blinds and, if called, usually retains postflop position.

This is why reasonable opening ranges expand toward the cutoff and button.

Effective stacks matter before the flop

Imagine you have $400 in a $1/$2 cash game, but your only likely opponent has $70. Although your physical stack is 200 big blinds, only $70, or 35 big blinds, is effectively at risk between you. Strategies that rely on winning a huge later pot when a disguised draw hits become less attractive when little money remains behind.

Conversely, very deep stacks make some hands with strong nut potential more interesting while making weak top-pair holdings more dangerous in enormous pots. The key is not simply “deep is good.” Depth magnifies future decisions.

Previous action matters

Poker vocabulary distinguishes several preflop entries:

An open is the first voluntary raise into an unopened pot. A limp means merely calling the big blind when nobody has raised. Calling a raise means matching someone else’s open. A three-bet is the next raise over an initial raise. The term comes from treating the blind as the first bet and the open raise as the second. Defending the blind broadly means continuing from a blind against a raise, either by calling or reraising.

A hand can be good enough to open but not good enough to call a strong raise. This is crucial.

Worked example: open-worthy does not mean call-worthy

You are on the button and everyone folds to you. K♠ 10♠ may be a perfectly reasonable opening hand because only two opponents remain, you can win the blinds immediately, and you will have position if called.

Change the situation. A very tight player raises from early position, another strong player reraises, and now you hold the same K♠ 10♠ on the button. The cards did not change, but the evidence about your opponents did. Their actions imply much stronger ranges. Calling because “K-10 suited is a good hand” confuses absolute card appearance with situational value.

Number of opponents and rake matter

The more players see a flop, the more likely somebody has connected strongly with it. Hands based mainly on one-pair strength generally lose relative value multiway, while very strong draws and nut-producing holdings may become more important. Cash-game rake can also make marginal calls less attractive because some of the pot is removed from the player economy. Cash-game commission methods are operator-specific, so strategic charts derived for one rake structure need not transfer perfectly to another.

Thinking in ranges

One of the most damaging beginner habits is trying to name an opponent’s exact cards: “He has ace-king.” Sometimes that guess is right by accident, but good reasoning usually asks a different question: What collection of hands could reasonably have taken this line?

That collection is a range.

Suppose a cautious player raises from first position. Before learning anything else, you might assign them a range containing strong pairs, strong aces, and good high-card combinations. If that same player calls a large reraise, some of their weakest opening hands may become less plausible. If they then call a substantial bet on an A-K-7 flop, their range changes again.

The range is not something you “discover” once. It is an estimate that must be updated after each new action.

Worked example: narrowing without pretending certainty

A player raises from early position. You call on the button. The flop is A♣ K♦ 7♠. The raiser bets.

You should not immediately conclude “ace-king.” Their preflop range could contain A-A, K-K, A-K, A-Q, other suited aces, Q-Q, J-J, and possibly bluffs depending on the player. Some of those hands bet this flop frequently; others may bet occasionally; some may check.

The turn is 2♥. They bet large again. Hands such as Q-Q and J-J may now feel less likely against many opponents because repeated large betting on this board often comes from stronger value or deliberate bluffs. But they are not impossible.

The river is Q♣ and the opponent bets again. You now reassess yet again. A-Q improved. J-10, if it was ever plausible, made a straight. Some earlier bluffs may still bluff. Range thinking keeps alternatives alive and weights them rather than pretending to see hidden cards.

Combinations and blockers

There are six possible combinations of pocket aces: A♠A♥, A♠A♦, A♠A♣, A♥A♦, A♥A♣, and A♦A♣. That is simply “four aces choose two.”

Suppose you hold one ace. Only three aces remain available, so an opponent can have only three combinations of A-A. Your known ace is therefore a blocker to pocket aces.

Blockers do not prove an opponent lacks a hand. They change how many versions are possible. For a beginner, that is enough. The aim is to replace “he cannot have it” with the more disciplined “my cards make some holdings less available.”

Draws, pot odds and expected value

Count outsPrice a river callCheck a turn draw

Probability becomes useful in poker when it answers a decision question. Knowing that a draw hits “sometimes” is not enough. You want to know how often, what it costs to continue, what you might win, and whether the cards you count as helpful actually produce the best hand.

Equity

Your equity is your share of the pot in probabilistic terms given assumptions about the hands or ranges involved and the cards still to come. If a heads-up all-in model gives you a 30 percent chance of an outright win and no ties, your equity is 30 percent. Ties add your expected share: a 20 percent chance to win plus a 20 percent chance to split a heads-up pot gives 20% + (20% × 1/2) = 30% equity. These are hypothetical probabilities, not frequencies measured from play.

Equity is not the same as guaranteed winnings. You can have 80 percent equity and lose this particular hand. Probability describes repeated uncertainty, not a promise about the next card.

Equity realization

A hand can possess theoretical equity yet fail to realize all of it because future betting may force it to fold before seeing the remaining cards. This distinction is especially important on the flop. Saying “my draw has about a one-in-three chance by the river” may be irrelevant if an opponent can make you pay again on the turn and you are not guaranteed to see the river.

Position, stack depth, vulnerability to future bets, and the possibility of being dominated all affect equity realization.

Outs

An out is an unseen card that improves you to what you expect to be the winning hand. A four-card flush draw normally appears to have nine flush outs because each suit contains thirteen cards and four are already known.

But an apparent out is not automatically a clean out. If the board is paired, a card that completes your flush may simultaneously allow an opponent’s full house to remain ahead. If an opponent can have a higher flush draw, some flush cards may help you make a losing flush. Good calculation therefore distinguishes raw outs from discounted outs, which are reduced to account for such problems.

The rule of two and four

A common mental shortcut estimates drawing probability by multiplying outs by about four when two cards are to come and by about two when only one remains. It is an approximation, not an exact formula. The outs lesson and math reference provide further examples.

Consider a nine-out flush draw on the flop. There are 47 cards unknown to you because you know your two hole cards and the three-card flop. For this simple draw-completion calculation, treat those 47 cards as equally possible turn cards. This does not condition on an opponent’s known hand or on information conveyed by their actions.

The exact probability of making the flush by the river, assuming nine target suit cards remain among the unknown cards and you get to see both cards, is:

Chance of completing the flush by the river = 1 - (38/47 × 37/46) ≈ 34.97%.

This is the chance of completing the flush, not automatically the chance of winning the pot. An opponent may already have or later make a stronger hand. The rule of four says 9 × 4 = 36%, a useful table estimate.

For the turn card alone, the exact probability is 9/47 ≈ 19.15%, while the rule of two gives 18 percent.

On the turn with one card left, 46 cards are unseen, so the exact probability is 9/46 ≈ 19.57%. Again, “18 percent” is merely a quick approximation.

The most important limitation is not the small numerical error. It is that multiplying by four on the flop is appropriate only when thinking about seeing both remaining cards. If you must call a flop bet now and may face another turn bet, the by-river percentage cannot simply be compared with the current price as though the river were free.

Pot odds

Pot odds compare the current pot with what a call costs. To convert that ratio to the required share of the final pot, use the call-cost calculation below.

If the pot contains P after an opponent bets and your call costs C, the break-even equity for a call with no future betting is:

Required equity = call cost / (current pot + call cost).

Be careful about definitions. Here P means the pot after the opponent’s bet but before your call.

Worked numerical example: pot odds

It is the river. The pot was $60 before your opponent acted. They bet $30.

The pot you are looking at is now:

$60 + $30 = $90.

Calling costs $30.

If you call, the final pot will be:

$90 + $30 = $120.

Therefore:

Required equity = 30 / 120 = 25%.

With no ties, you need to win more than 25 percent of the time, ignoring rake, to make the call positive in simplified chip or cash expected value. Another way to state the same price is that you are risking $30 to contest the $90 already out there, or 3-to-1 pot odds.

Because this example occurs on the river, there is no future betting to complicate the arithmetic.

Expected value

Expected value, usually abbreviated EV, asks what a decision would average if a sufficiently similar situation could be repeated many times. A positive-EV decision can lose today. A negative-EV decision can win today. That is why judging a poker choice solely from its result is conceptually wrong.

Worked numerical example: a one-card draw

You are on the turn with a flush draw. Assume, for teaching purposes, that all nine flush outs are clean and that if you call there will be no further betting. For example, the opponent’s $20 turn bet can be their remaining stack. This closes the future-price problem in the toy model. We know six cards and model the other 46 as equally possible river cards. We are not also specifying exact opponent cards; doing that would change the unseen-card count and potentially the outs. Assume we win on exactly those nine cards, lose on all others, and never tie. Then:

Chance of a winning target river card = 9 / 46 ≈ 19.57%.

Suppose the pot is $80 before the opponent bets. The opponent bets $20.

Current pot = $80 + $20 = $100.

Your call = $20.

Final pot after calling = $120.

Required equity:

Required equity = 20 / 120 ≈ 16.67%.

Under our simplified assumptions, your 19.57 percent chance exceeds the 16.67 percent price, so calling has positive expected value.

We can verify directly. If you hit, your net gain relative to the moment of decision is the $100 already in the pot. If you miss, you lose the $20 call.

EV = (9/46 × $100) - (37/46 × $20).

EV ≈ $19.565 - $16.087 = +$3.48.

That does not mean the call earns $3.48 every time. It means its average under these assumptions is approximately positive $3.48. In a real hand, dirty outs, rake, the opponent’s range, and future action can alter the result.

Implied odds

Current pot odds consider only money already available to win. Implied odds consider additional money you might win later if you improve. They can justify some calls that current pot odds alone do not, especially when stacks are deep and an improved hand could receive further action. But implied odds depend on estimates of future opponent behavior, so they are not guaranteed.

Reverse implied odds describe the opposite danger. You may improve enough to continue putting money in but still lose to an even stronger hand. Small flushes, weak top pairs, and the low end of vulnerable straights can create this problem.

Why bet, and how much?

Value betting

A bet is fundamentally a value bet when you expect worse hands to call often enough to make betting more profitable than checking. Notice the definition depends on the opponent’s calling range, not simply on whether your hand is “strong.”

Suppose you have top pair with an excellent kicker on the river. If an opponent will call with many weaker top pairs, a value bet can make sense. If the same opponent only calls with two pair or better and folds everything you beat, the exact same hand may not earn a value bet.

The right question is therefore not merely “Am I ahead?” It is “What worse hands call this size?”

Bluffing

A bluff is a bet intended primarily to make better hands fold. Bluffing is not magic and aggression is not automatically sophisticated. A bluff needs enough folds, considering its risk and reward, to compensate for occasions when it gets called.

Worked numerical example: break-even bluff frequency

The river pot is $100. You have a hand with effectively zero showdown value and bet $50 as a pure bluff. Assume that when called you always lose.

You risk $50 to win the $100 already in the pot.

Let f be the required fold frequency:

Break-even folds = risk / (risk + reward) = 50 / (50 + 100) = 1/3 ≈ 33.33%.

If the opponent folds exactly one-third of the time, the bluff breaks even before rake. More than one-third gives positive simplified EV; less gives negative EV. Under these assumptions, bluff EV is f × $100 - (1 - f) × $50. At f = 1/3 it is zero. If the opponent folds, your own $50 wager is returned with the pot; it is not an additional $50 of profit. This threshold compares bluffing with a check that earns zero in the model. It does not establish the best size against a real opponent.

Notice a useful contrast. A player calling a half-pot river bet needs 25 percent equity because the bet is added to the pot before the call. A player making a half-pot pure bluff needs one-third folds because they are risking half a pot to win one pot. These are different problems.

Semi-bluffs

A semi-bluff is a bet or raise made with a hand that is not currently strong enough to welcome a showdown but has meaningful ways to improve if called, such as a flush draw or straight draw. It can therefore win immediately through a fold or later by improving. This two-path logic is why draws are often natural bluff candidates.

That does not mean “always bet your draws.” If several players are in the pot, folds may be harder to generate. If a player rarely folds, the fold-equity component of the semi-bluff shrinks. If stacks are awkward, getting raised may be costly. Strategy always returns to ranges, price, position, and future streets.

Checking is an action, not an admission of defeat

Beginners often bet simply because checking feels passive. In reality, checking can protect a medium-strength hand from a large pot, induce an opponent to bluff, preserve weaker hands in an opponent’s range, take a free card with a draw, or maintain a balanced checking range.

“Bet to see where I am” is usually a poor primary reason. A bet spends money. Information obtained as a side effect may be useful, but paying for information without a clear value or bluff objective can become expensive.

Bet sizing

There is no universal correct size such as “always half pot” or “always raise to three big blinds.” Sizing changes the price offered to an opponent, the set of hands likely to continue, and the amount of stack available for future streets. An opponent’s calling and folding behavior at one size need not remain the same at another. Compare the options with those responses made explicit in betting with a purpose.

A small value bet may attract calls from weaker hands that would fold to a large bet. A larger bet may extract more money from a range that is strong enough to call anyway. A large bluff risks more but demands more from marginal bluff-catchers. The purpose of the bet must come before the size.

Stack depth and the changing board

Effective stacks in big blinds

Stack depth is often expressed in big blinds because that makes situations comparable across stakes. In a $1/$2 game, a $200 stack is:

Stack in big blinds = 200 / 2 = 100 BB.

If you have $200 but your opponent has $90, your heads-up effective stack is $90, or 45 big blinds.

The shortest relevant stack determines how much can ultimately enter the pot between those players. In a multiway hand, effective stacks can differ by opponent.

Stack-to-pot ratio

SPR, or stack-to-pot ratio, compares the effective stack remaining at the start of a postflop street with the current pot:

SPR = effective stack remaining / current pot.

If the flop pot is $40 and both relevant players have $160 behind, SPR is 4.

A low SPR means relatively little money remains compared with the pot, so strong one-pair hands can more often be worth committing with. A high SPR leaves room for several large bets, which makes very large pots more strongly associated with stronger ranges. This is a strategic tendency, not a commitment rule. A low ratio does not require you to call off a pair against every range. See the SPR definition and position and stacks guide.

Worked example: sizing changes future geometry

The flop pot is $40 and each player has $160 left. SPR is 4.

You bet $20 and your opponent calls.

New pot:

$40 + $20 + $20 = $80.

Each player has:

$160 - $20 = $140.

Turn SPR:

Turn SPR = 140 / 80 = 1.75.

One modest flop bet reduced SPR from 4 to 1.75. That is why bet sizing cannot be analyzed one street at a time. Today’s bet sets tomorrow’s stack and pot.

Shallow versus deep

When the effective stack is only 20 big blinds, there may not be room for three large postflop bets. Preflop raises consume a meaningful share of the stack, and top-pair type hands can be relatively powerful. At 200 big blinds, by contrast, enormous river bets remain possible. A single pair that was comfortable at shallow depth may be poorly suited to playing for the entire deep stack.

Deep stacks also amplify positional advantage because there are more consequential later decisions on which the in-position player can observe the opponent first.

A repeatable postflop process

Instead of memorizing a separate rule for every flop, ask the same sequence of questions:

  1. What is my actual five-card hand now, and what can it improve to?
  2. What hands can my opponent reasonably have after the earlier action?
  3. Which player’s range does this board help more?
  4. What worse hands call if I bet?
  5. What better hands might realistically fold?
  6. What price do I receive if facing a bet, or offer if making one?
  7. What turn or river cards materially change hand strength and future betting?

Those questions force the decision to connect hand strength, ranges, probability, and stack depth.

Board texture

A dry board offers relatively few immediate straight or flush draws, such as A♣ 7♦ 2♠. A coordinated or wet board such as J♥ 10♥ 9♣ supports many pairs, two-pair combinations, straights, and draws. These labels are shorthand, not precise mathematical categories.

On a dry A-7-2 rainbow flop, a preflop raiser who credibly holds many strong aces may retain a range advantage over a blind caller. On 9-8-7 with two hearts, a caller can plausibly have many two-pair combinations, sets, straights, pair-plus-draw hands, and flush draws. Betting strategy should reflect that difference rather than treating “I raised preflop” as permission to bet every flop automatically.

Continuation betting

A continuation bet, or c-bet, is a postflop bet by the player who had the betting initiative before the flop. Beginners sometimes treat it as mandatory. It is not. Board texture, number of opponents, ranges, position, stack depth, and sizing all matter. A preflop raise does not create an obligation to bet the flop.

Multiway pots

As additional players enter, the probability that at least one opponent has connected strongly tends to increase. Bluffing through three players generally requires more combined folding than bluffing through one. Value thresholds also rise because a call from one player does not end the action if others remain.

This makes multiway poker particularly unfriendly to automatic bluffing. For a beginner review, identify every remaining player and who can still raise before applying a heads-up calculation. The multiway workshop shows how eligibility and price change.

Worked example: relative hand strength changes with context

You hold A♠ Q♣ on A♦ 9♥ 4♣.

Heads-up against a big blind who called your preflop raise, top pair with queen kicker can be strong relative to an assumed broad calling range. Many worse aces, nines, pocket pairs, and backdoor holdings can exist. The actual betting line still matters; the label “big blind caller” is not a measured range.

Now imagine four opponents saw the same flop after several calls. Your absolute hand remains one pair of aces with queen kicker. But its relative strength falls because four ranges collectively contain more opportunities for A-K, A-9, A-4, 9-9, 4-4, and other strong holdings. The cards did not weaken. The competitive environment became stronger.

This is the recurring structure of poker decisions: hand strength is relational.

Cash games and tournaments

Different chip values

In a cash game, chips correspond directly to money under the room’s denomination system, blinds normally remain fixed for that table, and players can usually leave between hands and replenish stacks within house buy-in rules. Tournament players instead receive tournament chips, blinds rise according to a schedule, and prizes depend on finishing position. Tournament formats may be freezeouts, re-entry events, rebuy structures, bounty events, satellites, or other variants.

The distinction is not cosmetic. It changes decision incentives.

Cash games and tournaments
FeatureCash gameTournament
Chip meaningDirect cash denominationTournament accounting units
BlindsUsually fixed at chosen stakeIncrease by scheduled levels
Losing stackCan often rebuy within room rulesElimination unless structure permits rebuy or re-entry
LeavingUsually possible between handsNo cash-out of tournament chips; an absent stack normally keeps paying required blinds and antes
RewardChips won have direct monetary valuePrize depends on finishing position
Stack depthOften relatively stable by choiceFrequently changes as blinds rise
Payout pressureNone from finish positionCan become strategically important

Read the published structure for the actual event. The tournament formats guide explains the distinctions, and registration and re-entry keeps the total financial commitment visible.

Tournament survival matters, but not infinitely

Beginners sometimes hear “you cannot win a tournament if you bust” and conclude that chips should be protected at almost any cost. That is too simple. Chips are also the resource that lets you survive future blinds, pressure shorter stacks, and pursue higher finishes. A strategy that never takes profitable risks can be blinded away.

The proper tournament question is how chip gains and losses affect expected prize value under the particular stacks and payouts.

Independent Chip Model

The Independent Chip Model, or ICM, provides a way to estimate the prize-money value of tournament stacks from chip counts and the payout schedule. Tournament chips are not linearly convertible into cash because several finishing places may be paid. Doubling your chips therefore need not double your monetary tournament equity.

ICM becomes especially consequential around major payout changes, such as a money bubble or final table, although exact effects depend on all relevant stack sizes and prizes. The model also has limitations: a basic ICM calculation does not directly account for player skill, future position, or every structural feature of a tournament. The ICM introduction explains the model; the tournament equity guide supplies worked examples. Its results are model-dependent estimates, not a universal instruction to avoid elimination at any cost.

A beginner need not calculate complex ICM at the table. The conceptual lesson is enough initially: losing chips and gaining the same number of chips need not have symmetrical cash consequences in a tournament.

Opponents, variance and personal limits

Opponent tendencies

Two simple axes help organize observations.

A tight player voluntarily plays relatively few hands; a loose player plays many. A passive player tends to check and call more; an aggressive player bets and raises more.

These labels are descriptions, not identities. A normally tight player can bluff. An aggressive player can hold the nuts. Your objective is to use observed frequencies cautiously rather than turn them into stereotypes.

Suppose a player has called large river bets with weak pairs several times. A sensible adjustment may be to value bet more strongly and bluff them less. Suppose another player folds too often to modest river bets. More selective bluffing may become attractive.

The word cautiously matters. Three unusual hands are a tiny sample. Random cards themselves produce streaks. A few revealed hands are also a selected sample: you did not see every folded hand. Describe what you actually observed and keep an alternative explanation available. An opponent’s observed action is evidence, not proof of a permanent personality.

Balanced and exploitative strategy

A balanced strategy tries not to make its behavior so one-sided that an observant opponent can profit by using a simple counterstrategy. For example, if every huge river bet is always the nuts, opponents can fold everything else without concern. If every huge river bet is always a bluff, they can call very widely.

An exploitative strategy intentionally adjusts to an opponent’s mistakes. If somebody calls far too much, bluff less and value bet more. If somebody folds far too much, selectively bluff more.

Modern computational poker research demonstrates the importance of strategies that are difficult to exploit in imperfect-information games, but a beginner does not need to imitate solver outputs mechanically. The 2017 DeepStack paper studied heads-up no-limit hold’em. It is not evidence that multiway cash games or tournament prize decisions are solved, and it supplies no universal human opening chart. Use research or solvers with their game, assumptions, and evaluation scope stated.

Physical tells

Live behavior can be considered contextual evidence, but it should not be treated as mind reading. A trembling hand might mean nervousness, excitement, temperature, habit, or nothing strategically useful. Betting history, position, size, board texture, and an established behavioral baseline generally provide a more disciplined framework than a one-off gesture.

Variance

Imagine you move all-in as a strong favorite and an opponent hits one of a few remaining winning cards. Losing does not retroactively make the decision bad. Likewise, calling with terrible odds and hitting does not prove the call was good.

This is variance: actual short-run results fluctuate around underlying probabilities. The AIVAT paper studies reducing variance when evaluating agents in imperfect-information games, including poker. Its controlled agent-evaluation method should not be treated as a shortcut for estimating your own win rate from a small session record.

A useful learning habit is therefore to separate two questions:

What happened? You won or lost.

Was the decision justified by the information and price available at the time? That is the strategic question.

Bankroll and financial boundaries

A bankroll is money deliberately allocated to poker rather than money needed for housing, bills, food, debt obligations, emergency savings, or other necessities. There is no universal number of buy-ins that guarantees safety. The cushion appropriate to a player changes with format, stakes, game variance, uncertainty about skill, willingness to move down, and personal tolerance for financial risk.

Generic rules such as “always have exactly 20 buy-ins” should therefore not be treated as laws. A large-field tournament player may experience much larger result swings than a low-variance cash player. A recreational player who never intends to replenish poker money may choose a very different threshold from somebody managing a long-term playing bankroll.

GambleAware’s guidance recommends money and time limits and warns against chasing losses. These are boundaries, not a way to turn gambling into a safe investment. You can stop, lower the stakes, or choose study without wagering. For support information, use the site’s gambling-support directory. These safeguards matter independently of strategic skill. No starting-hand chart, probability calculation, or study routine guarantees profit.

Tilt means an emotional state that degrades decision making. Anger after a bad beat, urgency to recover losses, embarrassment, fatigue, and overconfidence after winning can all push a player away from their normal process. The most useful response is often not a clever tactical adjustment. It is to stop playing.

A predetermined time limit or loss boundary can help because the decision to stop is made before the emotionally charged situation arises. Chasing losses, by contrast, increases exposure precisely when judgment may be deteriorating.

Live poker procedure

At a live table, act only when it is your turn, keep your cards protected and visible to the dealer, make bets clearly, and ask the dealer or floor person whenever a procedure is unclear. Protect your cards, follow the action, and keep the relevant chips visible. If unsure, ask the dealer before making a declaration or releasing chips.

A string bet is an attempted bet or raise made through multiple chip movements without a prior clear declaration, such as pushing out calling chips and then reaching back for more after observing a reaction. Tournament procedures prohibit string bets and raises. Cash rooms commonly impose comparable restrictions, but the exact enforcement belongs to the house.

Clear verbal declarations solve many live beginner problems. Instead of silently moving an uncertain collection of chips, say “call,” “raise,” or “raise to fifty” before releasing chips. Official betting vocabulary and gestures can be binding when action is pending. Ask neutral questions before announcing your decision.

Do not expose or discuss live cards merely because you see players do it on television. Tournament rules may penalize revealing cards with action pending and enforce one-player-to-a-hand principles. Individual cash rooms can have different rules. The safest beginner practice is simple: keep your cards private until the hand is over or the dealer instructs you otherwise.

Online poker

Online play automates much of the procedure: the software tracks the pot, deals cards, enforces action order, and prevents illegal chip denominations. That removes some live errors but introduces others. Misclicks happen. Time banks expire. Multiple tables or faster dealing can create far more decisions per hour than a typical live session.

Software-assistance rules are platform-specific and can change. Never assume that a tool permitted for off-table study is permitted during play. PokerStars’ assistance policy prohibits real-time action advice and distinguishes some off-table tools from tools permitted during play. Other operators may be stricter about charts or reference material. The rules and fair-play guide points to the relevant authorities. TDA tournament procedures also prohibit using betting apps, charts, and outside strategy information at the table. A responsible player should check the current rules of the exact site rather than relying on an old forum post or another operator’s policy.

Common beginner mistakes and corrections

Common mistakes and possible corrections
MistakeWhy it happensBetter correction
Playing too many starting handsFolding feels boringPrefer stronger ranges, especially early
Ignoring positionCards feel more tangible than seat orderAsk who acts last before entering
Limping automaticallyCalling the blind seems cheapHave a reason for entering and understand raising options
Calling strong raises with dominated hands“My hand is normally playable”Reassess after every prior action
Overvaluing one pairTop pair looks visually strongJudge strength against board, range, and number of opponents
Chasing every drawImprovement feels possibleCompare clean outs with the actual price
Counting dirty outs as cleanAny improving card looks helpfulAsk whether the opponent can improve even more
Bluffing automatically after raising preflopContinuation betting becomes a habitConsider board, ranges, opponents, and fold likelihood
Bluffing several opponents too freelyThe bettor focuses on one callerAccount for the combined probability somebody continues
Failing to value betFear of being raisedAsk what worse hands can call
Betting “for information”Uncertainty feels uncomfortableBet primarily for value, folds, or a coherent strategic reason
Ignoring effective stacksPlayers look only at their own chipsUse the smaller relevant stack
Using one bet size mechanicallySimple rules are easier to rememberConnect size to ranges, board, price, and later streets
Acting out of turn liveInattention or nervesFollow the action and pause before moving chips
Judging decisions by outcomesWinning feels like proofReview information available before the result
Chasing lossesDesire to get evenStop at preset financial or time boundaries

Put the ideas into practice

Pause here and explain a changed situation before opening its answer. These checks ask what the rules and arithmetic establish. They do not ask you to guess an optimal strategy from missing information.

You posted a $2 big blind. A player raises to $9, and the action returns to you. How much more is a full call?

$7 more. Your $2 blind already counts toward the $9 wager: $9 - $2 = $7. Assume nobody raised again and you have sufficient chips. You cannot check while facing the additional amount. Knowing the price does not establish whether calling is good. If you counted another $9, revisit the chips-owed lesson, then try a raise to $11 instead: the additional call would be $9.

A heads-up river pot is $80 before an opponent bets $40. What is the break-even call price, and does it tell you to call?

The required share is 25%; the price alone does not tell you to call. The bet makes the current pot $120. Your extra $40 makes the final pot $160, so $40 / $160 = 25%. Assume no fees or side pots, enough chips to call, and no further betting after the call. You still need your equity against a justified betting range, including your share of any ties. If you divided by $120, revisit the river-call lesson. Try a changed bet of $20: the final pot is $120 and the price is about 16.67%.

You hold A♠ Q♦ against K♥ K♣ on Q♠ 9♥ 5♦ K♦ 2♣. Did your top pair on the flop stay ahead?

No. Rebuild both hands from the final seven cards. Your best five are Q-Q-A-K-9, a pair of queens. The opponent has K-K-K-Q-9, three kings, which wins. A strong flop description does not freeze the winner. If you kept the original label, revisit the changing-hand lesson. Then use a fresh case in the beginner checkpoint to explain the change without looking.

A realistic learning sequence

Start with mechanics. You should be able to look at seven cards and identify the best five without hesitation. Learn action order until you know instinctively who acts first before and after the flop. Practice pot counting.

Next, tighten preflop selection. Rather than memorizing hundreds of chart cells immediately, understand why early position requires more caution, why weak aces can be dominated, and why calling a raise is different from opening an unraised pot.

Then study pot odds. Practice the call-cost divided by final-pot calculation until it is automatic. Learn common draw counts, but train yourself to ask whether the outs are clean.

After that, introduce ranges. During hands, replace “What does she have?” with “What can she reasonably have?” Review how each action changes that collection.

Only then should more sophisticated concepts such as range advantage, polarization, blockers, sophisticated bluff selection, deeper ICM, and solver outputs become major study priorities. They are easier to understand when the foundations are already automatic.

A simple hand-review template

A private hand-review record
FieldWhat to record
FormatCash or tournament, live or online, table size
Stakes / blindsExample: $1/$2 or 500/1,000
Effective stackIn chips and big blinds
PositionsYour seat and relevant opponents
Hole cardsYour exact suits and ranks
PreflopEvery meaningful action and size
FlopBoard, pot, stack, action
TurnNew card, pot, stack, action
RiverNew card, pot, stack, action
Opponent rangeWhat seemed plausible at each stage
PricePot odds or risk/reward where relevant
AlternativesCheck, bet sizes, call, raise, fold
ReasoningWhy you chose the action
ResultRecord last, after analyzing the decision
LessonOne specific principle to carry forward

That ordering is intentional. Analyze the decision before dwelling on the result.

Worked review example

Suppose the river pot is $60 before an opponent bets $30. It is $90 after their bet, and you hold a bluff-catcher. Instead of writing “I called and he had a bluff, good call,” start with the information that actually mattered.

Your additional $30 call makes the final pot $60 + $30 + $30 = $120, so the break-even share is $30 / $120 = 25%, assuming no fees, no side pots, sufficient chips to call, and a call that ends betting. If the pot had instead been $90 before the same $30 bet, the final pot would be $150 and the price 20%. Labeling “before” and “after” avoids mixing those two situations. Now construct the opponent’s plausible river betting range. Which value hands reach the river this way? Which missed draws can bluff? Does this opponent historically underbluff or overbluff this line? Are there blockers in your hand? Only after making that estimate should you compare it with 25 percent. This review supplies no real opponent data, so “they can bluff” is not enough to justify the call.

Assume your hand beats every bluff, loses to every value hand, and never ties. A combination’s possibility does not tell you how often it reaches this bet; weight the opponent’s hands by the line and betting frequency. If the resulting weighted probability of a bluff you beat is below one quarter, folding may have been better even if this particular opponent happened to be bluffing. Conversely, if a sensible range estimate gives you more than 25 percent winning probability, the call may have been justified even when the opponent turns over a value hand.

This is how poker study becomes decision analysis rather than storytelling.

Use the hand-review sheet privately or review one fictional hand. After this guide, try two checkpoint situations without looking at the answers. If a reason is unclear, use the precise repair link and attempt a changed situation. Passing these examples does not establish profitable play.

The long-term goal is not to become certain. Poker does not offer certainty before hidden cards are revealed. The goal is to become better calibrated: to understand what is known, what is merely plausible, what the price is, what risks remain, and which decision has the strongest justification given those uncertainties.

That is why the central lesson of no-limit hold’em is broader than any starting-hand chart. The game combines probability, incomplete information, incentives, sequential decisions, and human behavior. Good players do not eliminate luck. They try to make better decisions while luck is still unresolved.
